bullets: In 1824, when Dickens was 12, his father **John Dickens was imprisoned for debt** in the Marshalsea prison.
Charles was sent to work at **Warren’s Blacking Warehouse**, labelling pots of boot polish for long hours. He felt abandoned and ashamed; he kept it secret for most of his life.
Link: the ‘solitary child, neglected by his friends’ in Stave 2 echoes Dickens’s own loneliness; the Cratchits reflect the respectable poor his family became.
By 1843 Dickens was famous but in financial trouble himself; the book was also meant to earn money (it sold out its first run of 6,000 copies by Christmas Eve).
core.h: Dickens’s life and why it matters
core.p: Charles Dickens (1812–1870) was the most popular novelist of the Victorian era. His childhood gave him first-hand knowledge of poverty.

bullets: London’s population grew rapidly; slums were overcrowded and disease-ridden.
The gap between the wealthy middle class and the urban poor was vast.
Many in the middle and upper classes believed poverty was the result of **laziness or moral failure**.
Economic thinking of **laissez-faire** (government should not interfere in the economy) and **Malthus**’s idea of ‘surplus population’ justified doing nothing.
core.p: The 1840s were a decade of economic depression, poor harvests, unemployment and hunger in Britain.

bullets: His aim: to make middle-class readers **feel** for the poor and **act** through charity and fairer treatment of workers.
The Preface hopes the ‘Ghostly little book’ will ‘haunt their houses pleasantly’: the story is designed to work on the reader as the ghosts work on Scrooge.
Scrooge **represents** the attitudes Dickens wanted to change; his transformation models the change Dickens wanted in his readers.

callouts.p: Dickens wanted to use the novella to persuade wealthy Victorian readers that the poor were not a ‘surplus population’ but fellow human beings for whom they were responsible.

core.p: In 1843 Dickens read the Second Report of the **Children’s Employment Commission** and visited the **Field Lane Ragged School** for poor children. He first planned a pamphlet, ‘An Appeal to the People of England on behalf of the Poor Man’s Child’, but decided a story would strike with far greater force.

bullets: Weak: ‘In Victorian times there were workhouses.’
Strong: ‘When Scrooge asks “Are there no prisons?”, Dickens puts the cold logic of the 1834 Poor Law into his mouth so that readers who shared that view would hear how heartless it sounds.’

summary: Dickens wrote A Christmas Carol (1843) as a ‘sledge-hammer blow’ for the poor: know his own childhood poverty, the social conditions of the ‘Hungry Forties’, and how his purpose (to change readers’ hearts and behaviour) shapes every stave.
